title: Apple SDE – Data prep
description_md: Your 60-question pattern bank from the Apple SDE–Data preparation, each question with its own tiny tables. Ordered from core semantics to dates, sequences and data-engineering patterns.

problems.title: Filter rows with several conditions
problems.statement_md: Return employee_id and name for department A employees with salary at least 80. Sort by employee_id.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** WHERE + AND / OR

**Grain:** one row = one qualifying employee.

**Watch out:** NULL salary does not satisfy salary >= 80; parenthesize mixed AND/OR rules.

solutions.label: WHERE + AND / OR
solutions.explain_md: Both predicates must hold on the same employee row.
solutions.sql:
SELECT employee_id, name
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'A' AND salary >= 80
ORDER BY employee_id;

problems.title: Distinct values
problems.statement_md: Return unique non-NULL cities, sorted alphabetically.

tables.name: customers
tables.description_md: One row per customer. city may be NULL.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** DISTINCT

**Grain:** one row = one city.

**Watch out:** DISTINCT applies to the entire selected row, not just its first column.

solutions.label: DISTINCT
solutions.explain_md: Two customers live in SF, but SF appears once.
solutions.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM customers
WHERE city IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY city;

problems.title: Find missing values
problems.statement_md: Return employee_id for employees with unknown salary, ordered by ID.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

hints_md: Output grain: one employee with missing salary.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** IS NULL

**Grain:** one row = one employee with missing salary.

**Watch out:** salary = NULL is never TRUE; zero salary and unknown salary are different.

solutions.label: IS NULL
solutions.explain_md: Finn has an unknown salary.
solutions.sql:
SELECT employee_id FROM employees
WHERE salary IS NULL ORDER BY employee_id;

problems.title: COUNT variations
problems.statement_md: Return total_rows, known_salaries, distinct_salaries for all employees.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** COUNT(*) / COUNT(column) / COUNT(DISTINCT column)

**Grain:** one row = one summary row.

**Watch out:** COUNT(column) and COUNT(DISTINCT column) exclude NULL.

solutions.label: COUNT(*) / COUNT(column) / COUNT(DISTINCT column)
solutions.explain_md: Six employees, five known salaries, and four distinct known salaries.

problems.title: Group and aggregate
problems.statement_md: Return dept, employee_count and total_salary by department, sorted by dept. Unknown salary contributes nothing to the sum.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** GROUP BY

**Grain:** one row = one department.

**Watch out:** SUM ignores NULL; an entirely NULL group would produce NULL, not zero.

solutions.label: GROUP BY
solutions.explain_md: GROUP BY collapses three employee rows into each department row.
solutions.sql:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS employee_count, SUM(salary) AS total_salary
FROM employees GROUP BY dept ORDER BY dept;

problems.title: Filter groups
problems.statement_md: Return customer_id and paid_total for customers whose paid orders total at least 100. Sort by customer_id.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** HAVING

**Grain:** one row = one qualifying customer.

**Watch out:** WHERE filters input rows; HAVING filters aggregate groups.

solutions.label: HAVING
solutions.explain_md: Filter paid rows first; then filter grouped totals.
solutions.sql:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS paid_total
FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100
ORDER BY customer_id;

problems.title: Conditional aggregation
problems.statement_md: Return customer_id, paid_count and cancelled_count for every customer represented in orders, sorted by customer_id.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

hints_md: Output grain: one customer represented in orders.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** SUM(CASE ...)

**Grain:** one row = one customer represented in orders.

**Watch out:** Customers with no orders require a separate customer table and LEFT JOIN.

solutions.label: SUM(CASE ...)
solutions.explain_md: Each status contributes a one or zero within its customer's group.
solutions.sql:
SELECT customer_id,
 SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_count,
 SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS cancelled_count
FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;

problems.title: Top N rows with deterministic ties
problems.statement_md: Return employee_id and salary for exactly three highest-paid employees. Exclude unknown salary; break salary ties by employee_id ascending.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** ORDER BY + LIMIT

**Grain:** one row = one selected employee.

**Watch out:** LIMIT 3 does not include every salary tie; use ranking when ties must be retained.

solutions.label: ORDER BY + LIMIT
solutions.explain_md: The 80 tie is resolved by smaller employee_id.

problems.title: Normalize and find duplicates
problems.statement_md: Ignore NULL emails. Return normalized_email and copies for normalized emails appearing more than once. Normalize by trimming spaces and lowercasing; sort by normalized_email.

tables.name: contacts
tables.description_md: One row per contact. Emails may be NULL; normalized duplicates are allowed.

hints_md: Output grain: one duplicated normalized email.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** LOWER + TRIM + HAVING

**Grain:** one row = one duplicated normalized email.

**Watch out:** Define normalization before counting; this contract does not remove internal whitespace.

solutions.label: LOWER + TRIM + HAVING
solutions.explain_md: Both spellings become a@x.com.
solutions.sql:
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized_email, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM contacts WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)) HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY normalized_email;

problems.title: Classify rows
problems.statement_md: Return employee_id and band: unknown for NULL salary, high for salary >= 90, otherwise regular. Sort by ID.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** CASE

**Grain:** one row = one employee.

**Watch out:** Do not silently classify NULL as a measured low value.

solutions.label: CASE
solutions.explain_md: CASE checks branches in order; missing values receive an explicit label.
solutions.sql:
SELECT employee_id,
 CASE WHEN salary IS NULL THEN 'unknown'
      WHEN salary >= 90 THEN 'high' ELSE 'regular' END AS band
FROM employees ORDER BY employee_id;

problems.title: Join matching rows
problems.statement_md: Return paid order_id, customer name and amount, ordered by order_id.

tables.name: customers
tables.description_md: One row per customer. city may be NULL.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** INNER JOIN

**Grain:** one row = one paid order.

**Watch out:** A customer may repeat: the result is at order grain, not customer grain.

solutions.label: INNER JOIN
solutions.explain_md: Each order matches at most one customer because customer_id is unique in customers.

problems.title: Include customers with zero orders
problems.statement_md: Return every customer_id and paid_orders, including zero, ordered by customer_id.

tables.name: customers
tables.description_md: One row per customer. city may be NULL.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** LEFT JOIN + COUNT(child key)

**Grain:** one row = one customer.

**Watch out:** Putting o.status in WHERE removes unmatched customers; COUNT(*) wrongly counts their placeholder.

solutions.label: LEFT JOIN + COUNT(child key)
solutions.explain_md: A LEFT JOIN retains all four customers; counting the child key ignores unmatched NULL placeholders.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS paid_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.customer_id ORDER BY c.customer_id;

problems.title: Customers who never paid
problems.statement_md: Return customer_id for customers with no paid orders, sorted by ID.

tables.name: customers
tables.description_md: One row per customer. city may be NULL.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

hints_md: Output grain: one customer without a paid order.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** NOT EXISTS

**Grain:** one row = one customer without a paid order.

**Watch out:** NOT IN can eliminate all results if its subquery contains NULL.

solutions.label: NOT EXISTS
solutions.explain_md: Ben has only a cancelled order; Dan has no orders.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
 WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid')
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

problems.title: Customers who paid at least once
problems.statement_md: Return each customer_id that has at least one paid order exactly once, sorted by ID.

tables.name: customers
tables.description_md: One row per customer. city may be NULL.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** EXISTS / semijoin

**Grain:** one row = one qualifying customer.

**Watch out:** Joining directly returns Ana twice unless you explicitly reduce the result.

solutions.label: EXISTS / semijoin
solutions.explain_md: EXISTS tests presence without multiplying customer rows.
solutions.sql:
SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
 WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'paid')
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

problems.title: Compare employee with manager
problems.statement_md: For every direct report with both their own and their manager's salary known, return employee_id, manager_id and exceeds_or_equals (1 when employee salary >= manager salary, otherwise 0). Sort by employee_id.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

hints_md: Output grain: one direct report with both salaries known.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Self join

**Grain:** one row = one direct report with both salaries known.

**Watch out:** A missing manager or unknown salary is excluded by the stated contract.

solutions.label: Self join
solutions.explain_md: Two aliases give the employee and manager separate roles; all three known direct-report salaries are below their managers.
solutions.sql:
SELECT e.employee_id, e.manager_id,
 CASE WHEN e.salary >= m.salary THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS exceeds_or_equals
FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary IS NOT NULL AND m.salary IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY e.employee_id;

problems.title: Above department average
problems.statement_md: Return employee_id and salary for employees earning strictly above their own department's average known salary; sort by ID.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Correlated subquery

**Grain:** one row = one qualifying employee.

**Watch out:** A global average answers a different question.

solutions.label: Correlated subquery
solutions.explain_md: A averages 260/3; B averages 150/2 because NULL is excluded.

problems.title: Avoid multiplying two child tables
problems.statement_md: For orders 101 and 102 return order_id, item_total and payment_total, sorted by order_id.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

tables.name: items
tables.description_md: One row per line item; many items per order. Amount is the whole line value.

tables.name: payments
tables.description_md: One row per payment. Orphan order 999 is deliberately allowed.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Pre-aggregate before joining

**Grain:** one row = one order.

**Watch out:** Order 101 has two items and two payments: a raw join makes four rows and doubles both sums.

solutions.label: Pre-aggregate before joining
solutions.explain_md: Reduce both many-side tables to one row per order before combining them.

problems.title: Find orphan records
problems.statement_md: Return payment_id and order_id for payments with no matching order, sorted by payment_id.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

tables.name: payments
tables.description_md: One row per payment. Orphan order 999 is deliberately allowed.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Anti join

**Grain:** one row = one orphan payment.

**Watch out:** Check a nonnullable parent key for missingness, not a nullable descriptive field.

solutions.label: Anti join
solutions.explain_md: Payment 4 points to absent order 999.

problems.title: Customers who bought every required product
problems.statement_md: Return customer_id for customers who purchased every product in required_products, sorted by ID. Repeated purchases do not count as different products.

tables.name: purchases
tables.description_md: One row per purchase; repeated customer/product combinations are allowed.

tables.name: required_products
tables.description_md: Nonempty set of required products, one row per product.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Relational division

**Grain:** one row = one qualifying customer.

**Watch out:** This contract assumes a nonempty required set. For an empty set and all customers, use customers plus double NOT EXISTS.

solutions.label: Relational division
solutions.explain_md: Customer 1 has A and B; repeating A alone is insufficient.
solutions.sql:
SELECT p.customer_id FROM purchases p
JOIN required_products r ON r.product_id=p.product_id
GROUP BY p.customer_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT p.product_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM required_products)
ORDER BY p.customer_id;

problems.title: Combine sources without losing duplicates
problems.statement_md: Return source, order_id for every orders row and every payments row, using source labels order and payment. Sort by source then order_id. Preserve repeated payment order IDs.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

tables.name: payments
tables.description_md: One row per payment. Orphan order 999 is deliberately allowed.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** UNION ALL versus UNION

**Grain:** one row = one source record.

**Watch out:** UNION removes duplicate selected rows even if they represent different underlying records.

solutions.label: UNION ALL versus UNION
solutions.explain_md: UNION ALL preserves the two separate payments for 101.
solutions.sql:
SELECT 'order' AS source, order_id FROM orders
UNION ALL
SELECT 'payment' AS source, order_id FROM payments
ORDER BY source, order_id;

problems.title: Second-highest distinct salary
problems.statement_md: Return the second-highest distinct known salary as second_salary. Always return one row; return NULL if it does not exist.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** DENSE_RANK

**Grain:** one row = one summary row.

**Watch out:** The second employee row is not necessarily the second distinct salary.

solutions.label: DENSE_RANK
solutions.explain_md: DENSE_RANK numbers distinct salaries without gaps; the final aggregate guarantees one row.

problems.title: Top two salary levels per department
problems.statement_md: Return dept, employee_id and salary for the top two distinct known salary levels in each department, including all ties. Sort by dept, salary descending, employee_id.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** DENSE_RANK PARTITION BY

**Grain:** one row = one qualifying employee.

**Watch out:** ROW_NUMBER would return at most two employees per department and drop a tied employee.

solutions.label: DENSE_RANK PARTITION BY
solutions.explain_md: Partition resets the ranking for each department. Both A employees at 80 qualify.

problems.title: Exactly one best employee per group
problems.statement_md: Return dept and employee_id for the highest-known-salary employee per department. Break ties by smallest employee_id; sort by dept.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

hints_md: Output grain: one department with known salary.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** ROW_NUMBER

**Grain:** one row = one department with known salary.

**Watch out:** Do not add employee_id to DENSE_RANK when salary ties must share rank.

solutions.label: ROW_NUMBER
solutions.explain_md: ROW_NUMBER plus a unique tie-breaker selects exactly one row.

problems.title: Understand ranking gaps
problems.statement_md: Return employee_id, salary, competition_rank and dense_rank_value for known salaries, sorted by salary descending then employee_id.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

hints_md: Output grain: one employee with known salary.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** RANK versus DENSE_RANK

**Grain:** one row = one employee with known salary.

**Watch out:** ORDER BY outside OVER controls display; ORDER BY inside OVER defines the ranking.

solutions.label: RANK versus DENSE_RANK
solutions.explain_md: The tie at rank 3 consumes two positions for RANK, so the next rank is 5.
solutions.sql:
SELECT employee_id, salary,
 RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS competition_rank,
 DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rank_value
FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY salary DESC, employee_id;

problems.title: Latest state with a tie-breaker
problems.statement_md: Return event_id, version_id and status for the newest version of every event. Compare updated_at first, then larger version_id; sort by event_id.

tables.name: versions
tables.description_md: One row per version. Use larger version_id to break equal updated_at ties.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Deduplication + ROW_NUMBER

**Grain:** one row = one logical event.

**Watch out:** MAX(updated_at) joined back can return multiple rows; filter status after choosing latest if asking for current status.

solutions.label: Deduplication + ROW_NUMBER
solutions.explain_md: Version 3 wins the timestamp tie for event 1.

problems.title: Running total
problems.statement_md: Return day, revenue and running_total from daily, sorted by day.

tables.name: daily
tables.description_md: One row per date; these four dates are consecutive. Revenue is non-NULL.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** SUM OVER + explicit ROWS frame

**Grain:** one row = one date.

**Watch out:** Aggregate to daily grain first if the input is transaction-level.

solutions.label: SUM OVER + explicit ROWS frame
solutions.explain_md: The window preserves daily rows while accumulating all earlier revenue.

problems.title: Compare with previous row
problems.statement_md: Return day, revenue and change_from_previous; first change is NULL. Sort by day.

tables.name: daily
tables.description_md: One row per date; these four dates are consecutive. Revenue is non-NULL.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** LAG

**Grain:** one row = one date.

**Watch out:** On sparse dates LAG means previous observed date, not necessarily yesterday.

solutions.label: LAG
solutions.explain_md: LAG reads the previous ordered row.

problems.title: Find next purchase
problems.statement_md: For every date_orders row return customer_id, order_id and next_order_id. Within a customer order by ordered_at then order_id; display by customer_id and ordered_at.

tables.name: date_orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All timestamps are UTC DATETIME; no implicit timezone conversion. Complete history for this fixture.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** LEAD

**Grain:** one row = one order.

**Watch out:** A window result must be filtered in an outer query or CTE in MySQL.

solutions.label: LEAD
solutions.explain_md: Partition prevents reading another customer's order; the last order has no successor.

problems.title: Share of total
problems.statement_md: Return dept, total_salary and pct_of_total rounded to two decimal places. Use known salaries only; sort by dept.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Aggregate then window total

**Grain:** one row = one department.

**Watch out:** An empty OVER means one overall window; PARTITION BY dept here would give each department 100%.

solutions.label: Aggregate then window total
solutions.explain_md: Department totals are divided by 410, the total across departments.

problems.title: Median without a percentile aggregate
problems.statement_md: Return median_score as the middle score for odd counts or average of the two middle scores for even counts. Scores are non-NULL.

tables.name: scores
tables.description_md: One row per observation; duplicate scores would be valid.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** ROW_NUMBER + COUNT OVER

**Grain:** one row = one summary row.

**Watch out:** MySQL 8 does not offer PERCENTILE_CONT as a built-in window function.

solutions.label: ROW_NUMBER + COUNT OVER
solutions.explain_md: For four values, positions 2 and 3 are 20 and 30, averaging to 25.

problems.title: All timestamps on a calendar day
problems.statement_md: Return order_id for orders on March 3, 2024 UTC, sorted by ID. Include every time on that date.

tables.name: date_orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All timestamps are UTC DATETIME; no implicit timezone conversion. Complete history for this fixture.

hints_md: Output grain: one order on the requested day.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Half-open day range

**Grain:** one row = one order on the requested day.

**Watch out:** BETWEEN '2024-03-03' AND '2024-03-03 23:59:59' can miss fractional seconds.

solutions.label: Half-open day range
solutions.explain_md: The interval includes March 3 midnight and excludes March 4 midnight.

problems.title: Previous calendar month in a leap year
problems.statement_md: As of March 15, 2024, return order_id for all orders in the previous calendar month, sorted by ID.

tables.name: date_orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All timestamps are UTC DATETIME; no implicit timezone conversion. Complete history for this fixture.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Month-start boundaries

**Grain:** one row = one February order.

**Watch out:** Previous calendar month is not the latest 30 days.

solutions.label: Month-start boundaries
solutions.explain_md: The range is February 1 through, but not including, March 1; leap day is naturally included.
solutions.sql:
WITH anchor AS (SELECT CAST('2024-03-15' AS DATE) AS as_of_day),
bounds AS (SELECT CAST(DATE_FORMAT(as_of_day,'%Y-%m-01') AS DATE) AS month_start FROM anchor)
SELECT o.order_id FROM date_orders o CROSS JOIN bounds b
WHERE o.ordered_at >= DATE_SUB(b.month_start, INTERVAL 1 MONTH)
 AND o.ordered_at < b.month_start ORDER BY o.order_id;

problems.title: Last three completed calendar days
problems.statement_md: As of March 4, 2024 at midnight UTC, return order_id from the three completed calendar days March 1–3. Exclude March 4; sort by ID.

tables.name: date_orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All timestamps are UTC DATETIME; no implicit timezone conversion. Complete history for this fixture.

hints_md: Output grain: one order in the range.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** DATE_SUB with exclusive today

**Grain:** one row = one order in the range.

**Watch out:** Including today changes both the window definition and its upper endpoint.

solutions.label: DATE_SUB with exclusive today
solutions.explain_md: The interval is March 1 00:00 through March 4 00:00 exclusive.
solutions.sql:
SELECT order_id FROM date_orders
WHERE ordered_at >= DATE_SUB(CAST('2024-03-04' AS DATE), INTERVAL 3 DAY)
 AND ordered_at < '2024-03-04'
ORDER BY order_id;

problems.title: Calendar days versus elapsed hours
problems.statement_md: For every job return id, calendar_days and full_hours. Keep NULL for unfinished jobs; sort by id.

tables.name: durations
tables.description_md: One row per job. ended_at may be NULL for unfinished jobs.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** DATEDIFF versus TIMESTAMPDIFF

**Grain:** one row = one job.

**Watch out:** DATEDIFF takes end,start and ignores time; TIMESTAMPDIFF takes unit,start,end and counts whole elapsed units.

solutions.label: DATEDIFF versus TIMESTAMPDIFF
solutions.explain_md: Job 1 crosses midnight but lasts only 45 minutes. Job 2 lasts 24 hours.

problems.title: Monthly totals without mixing years
problems.statement_md: Return month_key in YYYY-MM format and revenue from date_orders, sorted by month_key.

tables.name: date_orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All timestamps are UTC DATETIME; no implicit timezone conversion. Complete history for this fixture.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Year-month bucket

**Grain:** one row = one year-month.

**Watch out:** Grouping by MONTH alone mixes January of different years.

solutions.label: Year-month bucket
solutions.explain_md: Both February orders total 30; the four March orders total 180.

problems.title: Find month-end dates
problems.statement_md: Return order_id and month_end for orders whose UTC calendar date is the last date of their month, sorted by ID.

tables.name: date_orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All timestamps are UTC DATETIME; no implicit timezone conversion. Complete history for this fixture.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** LAST_DAY

**Grain:** one row = one month-end order.

**Watch out:** Month-end is not always the 30th or 31st; functions on indexed columns can affect access paths.

solutions.label: LAST_DAY
solutions.explain_md: February 29 is the last day of February 2024.
solutions.sql:
SELECT order_id, LAST_DAY(ordered_at) AS month_end FROM date_orders
WHERE DATE(ordered_at)=LAST_DAY(ordered_at) ORDER BY order_id;

problems.title: Week start and ISO week-year
problems.statement_md: Return day, monday_start and iso_yearweek for week_dates, ordered by day. Weeks start Monday; ISO week 1 follows the four-day rule.

tables.name: week_dates
tables.description_md: One row per date, covering an ISO week-year boundary.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** WEEKDAY + YEARWEEK mode 3

**Grain:** one row = one date.

**Watch out:** YEAR(day) plus WEEK(day) can label a year-boundary week incorrectly; WEEKDAY returns Monday=0.

solutions.label: WEEKDAY + YEARWEEK mode 3
solutions.explain_md: January 1, 2021 belongs to ISO week 53 of 2020.

problems.title: Parse date text
problems.statement_md: Return id and parsed_date from DD/MM/YYYY text, sorted by id. Inputs are guaranteed valid.

tables.name: date_text
tables.description_md: One row per text record. Both strings are valid DD/MM/YYYY dates.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** STR_TO_DATE

**Grain:** one row = one text record.

**Watch out:** STR_TO_DATE is not a complete cross-version validation strategy for arbitrary malformed dates; this exercise guarantees valid inputs.

solutions.label: STR_TO_DATE
solutions.explain_md: The format states day before month; output is a real date.
solutions.sql:
SELECT id, STR_TO_DATE(raw_date,'%d/%m/%Y') AS parsed_date
FROM date_text ORDER BY id;

problems.title: Age as of a fixed date
problems.statement_md: Return id and age_years on March 1, 2024, sorted by id.

tables.name: birthdays
tables.description_md: One row per person; dates are non-NULL.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** TIMESTAMPDIFF YEAR

**Grain:** one row = one person.

**Watch out:** Subtracting the birth year from the current year overstates age before the birthday.

solutions.label: TIMESTAMPDIFF YEAR
solutions.explain_md: Person 2's birthday has not happened yet in 2024.
solutions.sql:
SELECT id, TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR,birth_date,'2024-03-01') AS age_years
FROM birthdays ORDER BY id;

problems.title: Convert UTC before assigning business date
problems.statement_md: Using a fixed business offset of UTC−08:00, return order_id and business_day for order IDs 3 and 6. Sort by ID. This is a fixed-offset exercise, not a daylight-saving timezone.

tables.name: date_orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All timestamps are UTC DATETIME; no implicit timezone conversion. Complete history for this fixture.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** CONVERT_TZ then DATE

**Grain:** one row = one selected order.

**Watch out:** Real America/Los_Angeles reporting needs named-zone rules and loaded timezone tables; a fixed offset cannot model daylight saving.

solutions.label: CONVERT_TZ then DATE
solutions.explain_md: UTC midnight becomes 16:00 on the prior local date.
solutions.sql:
SELECT order_id, DATE(CONVERT_TZ(ordered_at,'+00:00','-08:00')) AS business_day
FROM date_orders WHERE order_id IN (3,6) ORDER BY order_id;

problems.title: Fill dates that have no sales
problems.statement_md: Return day and revenue for every date January 1–8, 2026. Missing sales mean zero; sort by day.

tables.name: sales_days
tables.description_md: One row per sale; multiple sales per day. No sales outside the displayed fixture.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Recursive calendar + LEFT JOIN

**Grain:** one row = one calendar date.

**Watch out:** Joining raw sales creates two January 3 rows; recursion needs a stopping condition.

solutions.label: Recursive calendar + LEFT JOIN
solutions.explain_md: Generate eight dates, aggregate sales at date grain, then attach totals.

problems.title: Trailing seven calendar days
problems.statement_md: Return day and rolling_7d only for January 7 and 8, 2026. Each total covers that day and the prior six calendar days. There are no earlier sales.

tables.name: sales_days
tables.description_md: One row per sale; multiple sales per day. No sales outside the displayed fixture.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Date spine + window + outer display filter

**Grain:** one row = one displayed date.

**Watch out:** Filtering to the displayed dates before the window loses required history. Seven rows means seven days only after filling dates.

solutions.label: Date spine + window + outer display filter
solutions.explain_md: January 7 includes Jan 1's 10 and Jan 3's 25; January 8 excludes Jan 1 and includes Jan 8's 30.

problems.title: Consecutive activity streaks
problems.statement_md: Return user_id, start_day, end_day and streak_days for all streaks of at least two consecutive active dates. Ignore duplicate events on the same date; sort by user_id, start_day.

tables.name: activity
tables.description_md: One row per activity event; duplicate user/day pairs are valid.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Gaps and islands

**Grain:** one row = one qualifying streak.

**Watch out:** Deduplicate user/day first; duplicate events otherwise break the date-minus-row-number technique.

solutions.label: Gaps and islands
solutions.explain_md: Subtracting consecutive row numbers from consecutive dates produces one constant key.
solutions.sql:
WITH d AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id,day FROM activity),
r AS (SELECT user_id,day,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day) AS rn FROM d),
g AS (SELECT user_id,day,DATE_SUB(day, INTERVAL rn DAY) AS island_key FROM r)
SELECT user_id,MIN(day) AS start_day,MAX(day) AS end_day,COUNT(*) AS streak_days
FROM g GROUP BY user_id,island_key HAVING COUNT(*)>=2
ORDER BY user_id,start_day;

problems.title: Sessionize event streams
problems.statement_md: Return event_id, user_id and session_no. A session starts on the first event or after an inactivity gap strictly greater than 30 minutes. Exactly 30 minutes stays in the same session. Sort by user_id,event_at,event_id.

tables.name: sessions
tables.description_md: One row per event. Order within a user by event_at, then event_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** LAG + break flag + cumulative SUM

**Grain:** one row = one event.

**Watch out:** TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE)>30 truncates 30 minutes 1 second to 30 and misses this boundary.

solutions.label: LAG + break flag + cumulative SUM
solutions.explain_md: 10:30 stays in session 1; 11:00:01 is 30 minutes and one second later, so starts session 2.
solutions.sql:
WITH previous AS (
 SELECT *, LAG(event_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at,event_id) AS previous_at
 FROM sessions
), flags AS (
 SELECT *, CASE WHEN previous_at IS NULL
 OR event_at>DATE_ADD(previous_at,INTERVAL 30 MINUTE) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS new_session
 FROM previous
)
SELECT event_id,user_id,SUM(new_session) OVER (
 PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_at,event_id
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS session_no
FROM flags ORDER BY user_id,event_at,event_id;

problems.title: Day-one cohort retention
problems.statement_md: Return signup_day, cohort_size, retained_users and retention_pct (two decimal places). Retained means activity exactly one calendar day after signup. Include zero-retention cohorts; sort by signup_day.

tables.name: signups
tables.description_md: One row per user. Observation is complete through January 5, 2026.

tables.name: activity
tables.description_md: One row per activity event; duplicate user/day pairs are valid.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Date equality + conditional distinct count

**Grain:** one row = one signup-date cohort.

**Watch out:** The denominator is signups, not active users. Exclude immature cohorts when the observation window is incomplete.

solutions.label: Date equality + conditional distinct count
solutions.explain_md: Only user 1 returns on January 2; user 2's January 3 activity is too late for day one.
solutions.sql:
SELECT s.signup_day, COUNT(DISTINCT s.user_id) AS cohort_size,
 COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS retained_users,
 ROUND(100.0*COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id)/COUNT(DISTINCT s.user_id),2) AS retention_pct
FROM signups s LEFT JOIN activity a
 ON a.user_id=s.user_id AND a.day=DATE_ADD(s.signup_day,INTERVAL 1 DAY)
GROUP BY s.signup_day ORDER BY s.signup_day;

problems.title: Month-over-month growth
problems.statement_md: Return month_start, revenue, previous_revenue and growth_pct rounded to two decimals. First-month growth and growth from a zero prior value are NULL. Sort by month_start.

tables.name: monthly
tables.description_md: One row per month, all months consecutive. Revenue is non-NULL.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** LAG + NULLIF denominator

**Grain:** one row = one month.

**Watch out:** On sparse monthly data, LAG reads the previous observed month; fill missing months first.

solutions.label: LAG + NULLIF denominator
solutions.explain_md: Growth is (current−previous)/previous. The input explicitly includes every month.

problems.title: Find missing activity dates
problems.statement_md: Return day for dates January 1–5, 2026 with no activity from any user. Sort by day.

tables.name: activity
tables.description_md: One row per activity event; duplicate user/day pairs are valid.

hints_md: Output grain: one missing calendar date.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Calendar anti join

**Grain:** one row = one missing calendar date.

**Watch out:** A filter on the activity table alone cannot manufacture missing dates.

solutions.label: Calendar anti join
solutions.explain_md: January 4 is absent from the complete set of observed activity dates.
solutions.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE calendar AS (
 SELECT CAST('2026-01-01' AS DATE) AS day
 UNION ALL SELECT DATE_ADD(day,INTERVAL 1 DAY) FROM calendar WHERE day<'2026-01-05'
)
SELECT c.day FROM calendar c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM activity a WHERE a.day=c.day)
ORDER BY c.day;

problems.title: Rolling distinct active users
problems.statement_md: Return day and active_users_3d for January 3, 4 and 5. Count distinct users active on that date or the previous two dates, including zero if none. Sort by day.

tables.name: activity
tables.description_md: One row per activity event; duplicate user/day pairs are valid.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Range join + COUNT DISTINCT

**Grain:** one row = one reporting date.

**Watch out:** Adding daily distinct counts double-counts returning users; MySQL does not support COUNT(DISTINCT ...) as a window aggregate.

solutions.label: Range join + COUNT DISTINCT
solutions.explain_md: Deduplicate user IDs across each entire three-day interval.
solutions.sql:
WITH report_days AS (
 SELECT CAST('2026-01-03' AS DATE) AS day
 UNION ALL SELECT CAST('2026-01-04' AS DATE)
 UNION ALL SELECT CAST('2026-01-05' AS DATE)
)
SELECT r.day,COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS active_users_3d
FROM report_days r LEFT JOIN activity a
 ON a.day>=DATE_SUB(r.day,INTERVAL 2 DAY) AND a.day<=r.day
GROUP BY r.day ORDER BY r.day;

problems.title: Repeat purchase within seven elapsed days
problems.statement_md: Return customer_id for customers whose second-ever order occurs no more than seven elapsed days after their first. Ties use order_id; include an exact seven-day boundary. Sort by ID.

tables.name: date_orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All timestamps are UTC DATETIME; no implicit timezone conversion. Complete history for this fixture.

hints_md: Output grain: one qualifying repeat customer.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** ROW_NUMBER + first/second timestamps

**Grain:** one row = one qualifying repeat customer.

**Watch out:** This is first-to-second order conversion, not any pair of orders within seven days; avoid truncated day differences.

solutions.label: ROW_NUMBER + first/second timestamps
solutions.explain_md: Both customers 1 and 2 have a second order within seven elapsed days; customer 3 has no second order.
solutions.sql:
WITH r AS (
 SELECT *,ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_at,order_id) AS rn
 FROM date_orders
), first_two AS (
 SELECT customer_id,
 MAX(CASE WHEN rn=1 THEN ordered_at END) AS first_at,
 MAX(CASE WHEN rn=2 THEN ordered_at END) AS second_at
 FROM r WHERE rn<=2 GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id FROM first_two
WHERE second_at<=DATE_ADD(first_at,INTERVAL 7 DAY)
ORDER BY customer_id;

problems.title: Count weekdays in an interval
problems.statement_md: For each completed job return id and weekday_count, counting Monday–Friday calendar dates from DATE(started_at) through DATE(ended_at), inclusive. Exclude unfinished jobs. No holiday exclusions; sort by id.

tables.name: durations
tables.description_md: One row per job. ended_at may be NULL for unfinished jobs.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Calendar generation + WEEKDAY

**Grain:** one row = one completed job.

**Watch out:** This counts calendar weekdays, not eight-hour working periods. Holiday handling requires a holiday calendar.

solutions.label: Calendar generation + WEEKDAY
solutions.explain_md: February 28 and 29, 2024 are Wednesday and Thursday; both dates count under an inclusive-date contract.
solutions.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE dates AS (
 SELECT id,DATE(started_at) AS day,DATE(ended_at) AS end_day
 FROM durations WHERE ended_at IS NOT NULL
 UNION ALL
 SELECT id,DATE_ADD(day,INTERVAL 1 DAY),end_day FROM dates WHERE day<end_day
)
SELECT id,SUM(CASE WHEN WEEKDAY(day)<5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS weekday_count
FROM dates GROUP BY id ORDER BY id;

problems.title: Detect overlapping intervals
problems.statement_md: Return id1,id2 for each overlapping interval pair once, smaller ID first. Touching endpoints do not overlap. Sort by id1,id2.

tables.name: intervals
tables.description_md: One row per valid interval [start_at,end_at); start is included, end excluded. Nested intervals occur.

hints_md: Output grain: one overlapping unordered pair.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Self join with strict boundaries

**Grain:** one row = one overlapping unordered pair.

**Watch out:** Using <= includes touching intervals; omit a.id<b.id and you get self-pairs plus reversed duplicates.

solutions.label: Self join with strict boundaries
solutions.explain_md: Two half-open intervals overlap when each begins before the other ends.
solutions.sql:
SELECT a.id AS id1,b.id AS id2 FROM intervals a
JOIN intervals b ON a.id<b.id
 AND a.start_at<b.end_at AND b.start_at<a.end_at
ORDER BY id1,id2;

problems.title: Merge nested and overlapping intervals
problems.statement_md: Return merged_start and merged_end for merged intervals, sorted by merged_start. Merge overlaps transitively; keep touching intervals separate.

tables.name: intervals
tables.description_md: One row per valid interval [start_at,end_at); start is included, end excluded. Nested intervals occur.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Running MAX endpoint + islands

**Grain:** one row = one merged interval.

**Watch out:** LAG(end_at) alone fails for nested intervals. Change >= to > only if touching intervals should merge.

solutions.label: Running MAX endpoint + islands
solutions.explain_md: The running maximum remembers interval 1's endpoint 10 despite nested interval 2 ending at 3. Interval 3 extends the merged interval to 12.

problems.title: Traverse an employee hierarchy
problems.statement_md: Return employee_id and depth for employee 1 and all their descendants, with the root at depth 0. Sort by depth,employee_id. Assume an acyclic hierarchy.

tables.name: employees
tables.description_md: One row per employee; salary and manager_id may be NULL. Other fields are non-NULL. A manager_id references employee_id.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** WITH RECURSIVE

**Grain:** one row = one reachable employee.

**Watch out:** Cycles require explicit detection in less constrained data; recursion has a configured depth limit.

solutions.label: WITH RECURSIVE
solutions.explain_md: The anchor selects the root; each recursion step finds reports of the prior level.
solutions.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE team AS (
 SELECT employee_id,0 AS depth FROM employees WHERE employee_id=1
 UNION ALL
 SELECT e.employee_id,t.depth+1 FROM employees e
 JOIN team t ON e.manager_id=t.employee_id
)
SELECT employee_id,depth FROM team ORDER BY depth,employee_id;

problems.title: Ordered event funnel
problems.statement_md: Return user_id, view_at, cart_at and purchase_at for users who complete view → cart → purchase in strictly increasing time order. Choose earliest view, earliest cart after it, and earliest purchase after that; sort by user_id.

tables.name: events
tables.description_md: One row per event; event timestamps determine funnel order. All fields non-NULL.

hints_md: Output grain: one completed user funnel.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Stage CTEs with temporal joins

**Grain:** one row = one completed user funnel.

**Watch out:** Independent MIN timestamps per event kind can misclassify funnels; the stages must be temporally related.

solutions.label: Stage CTEs with temporal joins
solutions.explain_md: User 2 purchased before viewing and does not complete the specified ordered sequence.

problems.title: Pivot event rows into columns
problems.statement_md: For each user return user_id, first_view_at and first_purchase_at independently. Keep NULL when an event kind is absent; sort by user_id. This question does not require funnel order.

tables.name: events
tables.description_md: One row per event; event timestamps determine funnel order. All fields non-NULL.

hints_md: Output grain: one user represented in events.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** MIN(CASE ...) pivot

**Grain:** one row = one user represented in events.

**Watch out:** This pivot is not proof of an ordered funnel; MySQL has no general PIVOT keyword.

solutions.label: MIN(CASE ...) pivot
solutions.explain_md: Conditional MIN puts the first occurrence of each kind in its own column.
solutions.sql:
SELECT user_id,
 MIN(CASE WHEN kind='view' THEN event_at END) AS first_view_at,
 MIN(CASE WHEN kind='purchase' THEN event_at END) AS first_purchase_at
FROM events GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY user_id;

problems.title: Reconcile both sides, including orphans
problems.statement_md: Return order_id, order_amount, payment_total and difference = order_amount − payment_total for every key in either orders or payments. Treat a missing side as zero; include all order statuses and sort by order_id.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

tables.name: payments
tables.description_md: One row per payment. Orphan order 999 is deliberately allowed.

hints_md: Output grain: one order key from either source.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Full outer join emulation

**Grain:** one row = one order key from either source.

**Watch out:** MySQL does not support FULL OUTER JOIN syntax; a one-sided LEFT JOIN would lose orphan payment 999.

solutions.label: Full outer join emulation
solutions.explain_md: The union of keys retains records appearing on either side. Payment aggregation ensures one row per key.

problems.title: Point-in-time dimension lookup
problems.statement_md: Return sale_id and tier that was valid on each sale_day, ordered by sale_id. Keep a sale with NULL tier if no version matches.

tables.name: facts
tables.description_md: One row per sale; customer_id references versioned history.

tables.name: history
tables.description_md: Nonoverlapping versions per customer with [valid_from,valid_to); NULL end is unbounded.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** As-of range join / SCD type 2

**Grain:** one row = one sale.

**Watch out:** BETWEEN on both inclusive endpoints can match two versions; overlapping history must be rejected or resolved.

solutions.label: As-of range join / SCD type 2
solutions.explain_md: January 31 maps to silver; February 1 is excluded from silver and included in gold.
solutions.sql:
SELECT f.sale_id,h.tier FROM facts f
LEFT JOIN history h ON h.customer_id=f.customer_id
 AND f.sale_day>=h.valid_from AND (f.sale_day<h.valid_to OR h.valid_to IS NULL)
ORDER BY f.sale_id;

problems.title: Weighted average
problems.statement_md: Return weighted_average to two decimal places. Use value weighted by weight, not the plain mean.

tables.name: weighted
tables.description_md: One row per observation; positive weights.

problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Ratio of sums

**Grain:** one row = one summary row.

**Watch out:** AVG(value) gives 15, ignoring weights. Protect against a zero denominator when that is possible.

solutions.label: Ratio of sums
solutions.explain_md: The numerator is 10×1 + 20×3 = 70; total weight is 4.
solutions.sql:
SELECT ROUND(1.0*SUM(value*weight)/NULLIF(SUM(weight),0),2) AS weighted_average
FROM weighted;

problems.title: First time a cumulative threshold is reached
problems.statement_md: Return id and running_total for the earliest transaction at which the cumulative amount is at least 60. Order is id ascending. If never reached, return no rows.

tables.name: balances
tables.description_md: One row per transaction; id defines transaction order.

hints_md: Output grain: one first crossing transaction, or none.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Running SUM + first qualifying row

**Grain:** one row = one first crossing transaction, or none.

**Watch out:** Filtering source transactions before computing the running total changes the balance.

solutions.label: Running SUM + first qualifying row
solutions.explain_md: The running balances are 40,70,120, so transaction 2 is the first crossing.

problems.title: Smallest set contributing at least 80 percent
problems.statement_md: Return customer_id, paid_total and cumulative_pct (two decimals) for the smallest leading set of customers reaching at least 80% of paid revenue. Sort by paid_total descending then customer_id; include the row that crosses 80%. Paid amounts are positive.

tables.name: orders
tables.description_md: One row per order. All fields non-NULL. customer_id references customers; one customer can have many orders.

hints_md: Output grain: one customer in the selected leading set.
problems.notes_md:
**Pattern family:** Aggregate + descending cumulative share

**Grain:** one row = one customer in the selected leading set.

**Watch out:** Filtering cumulative_pct<=80 drops the crossing row and fails to reach the target; positive values are essential for monotonic accumulation.

solutions.label: Aggregate + descending cumulative share
solutions.explain_md: Customer 1 contributes 150/190, below 80%, so customer 3 must be included to cross the threshold.
solutions.sql:
WITH totals AS (
 SELECT customer_id,SUM(amount) AS paid_total FROM orders
 WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY customer_id
), r AS (
 SELECT *,SUM(paid_total) OVER () AS grand_total,
 SUM(paid_total) OVER (ORDER BY paid_total DESC,customer_id
 ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total
 FROM totals
)
SELECT customer_id,paid_total,
 ROUND(100.0*running_total/NULLIF(grand_total,0),2) AS cumulative_pct
FROM r WHERE running_total-paid_total < 0.8*grand_total
ORDER BY paid_total DESC,customer_id;
